title: IRS hands down final auto enrollment rules for new 401(k), 403(b) plans

 IRS hands down final auto enrollment rules for new 401(k), 403(b) plans
 Treasury’s final SECURE 2.0 regulations give plan sponsors flexibility, though Vanguard calls for existing plans to face the mandate too
 NOV 17, 2026
 By  
 Leo Almazora
 The Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service have finalized the rules behind SECURE 2.0’s automatic enrollment mandate, spelling out how employers with newer 401(k) and 403(b) plans must sign workers up by default and giving plan sponsors more room in how quickly those contributions rise.
 Under the final regulations, covered plans generally must enroll eligible employees at a 3% contribution rate. After an initial period, that default has to climb by at least one percentage point a year until it reaches at least 10%, with a 15% ceiling. Workers keep the right to opt out or pick a different rate. The rules generally take effect for plan years starting in 2028.
 Treasury estimates the automatic enrollment expansion will add an average of $4.2 billion a year to retirement savings through 2032.
 “Today’s rules help more American families and workers build retirement savings while keeping them in control of their contributions and give employers the clarity and flexibility to invest in their employees’ futures,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement announcing the new rules .
 What the final automatic enrollment rules change
 The package clarifies the statutory carve-outs for qualifying small and new businesses, governmental plans, church plans and SIMPLE 401(k) plans. It also gives sponsors leeway on the timing and size of annual increases, within the limits Congress set, and explains how the mandate applies after plan mergers.
 The new rules open the door to less paperwork for plan sponsors. Certain required notices can be combined, and eligible employees who aren’t participating will face fewer annual notices, as long as they receive yearly reminders and any plan documents they’re entitled to request.
 “These regulations reduce the administrative burden placed on taxpayers when making long-term financial decisions,” said Frank J. Bisignano, the IRS’s chief executive officer.
 Read more:   Small businesses' retirement-plan readiness splits on generational, gender lines 
 The final version follows draft guidance on auto enrollment and catch-up contributions that the agencies floated nearly two years ago.
 The National Association of Insurance and Financial Advisors praised the rules for giving employers firm guidance.
 “Automatic enrollment is a proven way to encourage retirement savings, particularly among workers who might otherwise delay participating in an employer-sponsored plan,” Kevin Mayeux, NAIFA’s chief executive, said in a statement following the new ruls .
 Where Vanguard wants policymakers to go next
 The rules land as Vanguard pushes Washington to go further. In a policy research paper published prior to the new rules, the asset manager argued the auto-enrollment mandate should extend to existing employer plans, not just newer ones, with small businesses exempt and periodic re-enrollment for workers who opted out.
 Based on its own data, Vanguard said plans with automatic enrollment exhibit participation rates at roughly 94%, compared to 64% in plans where workers have to sign up. The firm estimates that broadening the requirement could add about 16.6 million participants and roughly $186,000 in savings by age 65 for a worker who stays enrolled across a career.
 Read more:   401(k) plans have boosted workers' retirement readiness, ICI report finds 
 Aside from that, Vanguard called for a 6% default saving rate, double the 3% the rules generally require. Its research found job switchers moving into plans with a 2% default saw their saving rate fall a median 2.4 percentage points, while those entering 6% plans saw a slight gain. About 31% of plans it administers already default at 6% or higher.
 "[S]ome workers, particularly lower earners and those facing financial constraints, may partially offset larger retirement contributions by increasing borrowing, while others may opt out entirely," the paper's authors conceded. 
 "Policymakers and plan sponsors should therefore preserve simple options to opt out or reduce the contribution rate, monitor differential effects across income groups, and consider gradual escalation to the higher default rate," they added.
